title: Fatigue, nausea and weight loss in a woman with diabetes

source.citation: Almascati Y, Alhumaiqani A. Euglycemic Diabetic Ketoacidosis Triggered by Sodium-Glucose Cotransporter 2 (SGLT2) Inhibitor Use in a Patient With Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus. Cureus. 2025;17(5):e84170.

presentation.hpi: Fatigue worsening over one month, with intermittent mild abdominal discomfort, persistent nausea, poor appetite and an unintentional weight loss of about 7 kg. Two months ago a newly consulted physician abruptly stopped her long-standing basal-bolus insulin and switched her to oral agents; she blames the nausea on the new tablets but has kept taking them.

exam: No guarding, rebound tenderness or organomegaly

diagnosis.primary: Euglycemic diabetic ketoacidosis associated with an SGLT2 inhibitor (empagliflozin) after insulin was stopped

management: Low-dose intravenous insulin infusion with dextrose-containing fluids and potassium replacement
All oral agents, including the SGLT2 inhibitor, withheld
outcome: Recovered; after stabilization she was transitioned back to a basal-bolus insulin regimen.
teachingPoints: SGLT2 inhibitors can cause ketoacidosis with a glucose below 250 mg/dL (14 mmol/L): check ketones and the anion gap in any unwell patient taking one.
Insulin deficiency, here stopping insulin in a patient with a low C-peptide, is a classic precipitant.
Treat with insulin plus dextrose-containing fluids so insulin can continue while the glucose stays normal; correct a low potassium before starting insulin.

questions.extra: Venous pH 7.30, bicarbonate 15 mmol/L, anion gap 21 mmol/L, glucose 7 mmol/L (126 mg/dL), potassium 3.2 mmol/L. Urine ketones 4+, serum ketones strongly positive.
questions.explanation: A high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis (pH 7.30, bicarbonate 15) with strongly positive ketones and a glucose below 250 mg/dL (14 mmol/L) is euglycemic DKA. Starvation ketosis rarely drops the bicarbonate below about 18 mmol/L, lactic acidosis needs a raised lactate, and renal tubular acidosis has a normal anion gap.

questions.q: Which of her medicines is most strongly associated with this presentation?
questions.explanation: SGLT2 inhibitors such as empagliflozin lower glucose through glycosuria, so ketoacidosis can develop with a near-normal glucose, especially with insulin deficiency, fasting, illness or surgery. Stopping her basal-bolus insulin (C-peptide 0.88 ng/mL suggests limited insulin reserve) set the scene.

options: IV insulin with dextrose-containing fluids and potassium replacement
Insulin infusion alone, stopped once the glucose is normal
questions.explanation: Ketoacidosis needs insulin until the ketones clear and the anion gap closes, and dextrose-containing fluids let it continue without hypoglycemia. Replace potassium first: insulin is held until potassium is above about 3.3–3.5 mmol/L (ADA hyperglycemic crises consensus). Stop the SGLT2 inhibitor.

evidence.quote: A 53-year-old female with a known history of T2DM
presented to the emergency department with a primary complaint of progressive fatigue that had been worsening over one month
She also reported intermittent mild abdominal discomfort, persistent nausea, reduced appetite, and unintentional weight loss of approximately 7 kg
Two months prior to presentation, her longstanding basal-bolus insulin regimen was abruptly discontinued on the recommendation of a newly consulted physician.
She reported worsening nausea, which she attributed to the new oral medications, but remained adherent to the prescribed regimen.
Instead, she switched to antihyperglycemic agents, including a combination of glimepiride/metformin, pioglitazone, and empagliflozin.
blood pressure of 126/74 mmHg, heart rate of 88 beats per minute, respiratory rate of 17 breaths per minute
oxygen saturation of 98% on room air, and temperature of 36.8 degrees Celsius
There was mild epigastric tenderness on palpation, but no guarding, rebound tenderness, or organomegaly.
Glucose 7 mmol/L
Venous pH 7.30
Bicarbonate 15 mmol/L
Anion gap 21 mmol/L
initial serum potassium level of 3.2 mmol/L guided potassium replacement
Urinalysis 4+ ketones
Serum and urine ketones were strongly positive.
an elevated HbA1c at 9.0%
a C-peptide level of 0.88 ng/ml
high anion gap metabolic acidosis in the setting of near-normal blood glucose levels
No evidence of infection, dietary restriction, recent illness, or medication non-adherence was identified.
started on a low-dose intravenous insulin infusion protocol in combination with dextrose-containing intravenous fluids and potassium replacement
All oral antihyperglycemic agents, including the SGLT2 inhibitor, were withheld upon admission.
After stabilization, she was safely transitioned back to a basal-bolus insulin regimen.
